card lp-rubric  [decided]
Two rubrics, prototype and production, built into the tool
why: A loop needs a stop condition. It differs by whether the output is thrown away or merged, but not by work item — so there are two of them, and neither is re-derived per run.
subtree: 2 cards, 2 decided, 1 unchallenged, 1 stale

A rubric is the loop's stop condition. There are two, and the loop picks by what happens to the output: #lp-rubric-proto when the artifact is thrown away after it answers a question, #lp-rubric-prod when the code is merged.

**Both are built into werk.** Not files in the repo being judged, not drafted per project, not derived per work item. Two constants the tool ships with.

Each has three sections, and the split is what makes a rubric usable:

    checks        deterministic — a command, an exit code, no model (#lp-two)
    judgements    an agent grades each, because no exit code answers them
    held-out      withheld from the builder, run once at the end (#lp-split)

The production rubric has all three. The prototype rubric has no held-out section — held-out exists to stop a builder gaming a bar it can see, and a throwaway accumulates nothing worth gaming.

**Written once, not per work item.** That is the property the rejected options give up. A rubric re-derived per run needs approval per run, and the recurring human input is exactly what the rubric exists to remove.

**The cost of hardcoding, stated so it is not a surprise.** #lp-rubric-prod's checks name `bun`, `tsc` and playwright; its judgements name `.werk/log.jsonl` and the werk CLI. Pointing the loop at a second project means editing werk's source. That is the moment #lp-rubric:opt3 stops being deferred.

Deferred: #lp-rubric:opt3 (a prototype.md and production.md file in each project, drafted from the repo and corrected once). Not rejected — it is what the hardcoded pair becomes once a second project exists.

Rejected: #lp-rubric:opt0 (derived per work item, approved at a gate). #lp-rubric:opt1 (project baseline plus per-item additions — the per-item part is where a builder would negotiate its own bar).

card werk-loop-done  [open]
The inner-loop stop condition for v0
why: The inner loop stops when the production rubric's checks pass. A retry cap decides what happens when they do not.

One pass over one ticket ends in one of three states: the checks pass, the checks fail and a retry remains, or the cap is reached.

The checks are #lp-rubric's `production` block, not a new list:

    bun test
    bun test --coverage      90% on fold.ts, log.ts, permission.ts, types.ts
    bun run e2e
    tsc --noEmit

On a fail, the next pass is a fresh agent with the same brief plus the last failure, per #lp-stateless. Nothing else carries over.

On the cap, stop the run and leave the branch where it is. Do not move to the next ticket with a broken tree underneath it — a second ticket built on a red base makes the failure harder to attribute, not easier.

**What a builder pass does not run.** The `judgements` block and the `held-out` block of the same rubric. Judgements need a grader agent, which is #lp-two, still open. Held-out is withheld from the builder by definition and belongs to #werk-loop-merge, which runs after the merge on a tree no single builder controls.

So the builder's bar is exit codes only. The graded and held-out bars exist and are placed; they are just not this pass's job.

Open: the retry number.

The plan is detailed. It is not complete. Every unit will hit something the cards do not settle — a name, a file split, an error case.

Three ways this can go, and only the third keeps both properties Eryk asked for:

1. The agent stops and asks. Kills autonomy. Out.
2. The agent picks and says nothing. Keeps autonomy, loses the decision — the map now lies about what was decided, and the next pass cannot see the pick.
3. The agent picks, and the pick becomes a card: who:prototype, status open, parented under the unit it came from, with the reading it chose in the body.

3 is already werk's own convention — `--who prototype` exists in `werk add` for exactly this. It also turns the build into a source of planning work instead of a consumer of it: after a run, `werk find` shows Eryk what the loop had to invent.

#al-sample is the related mechanism one layer up, at plan time. This is its build-time counterpart: plan-time sampling asks a human, build-time picking tells a human afterwards.

Inner build loop
why: A selected subtree of decided cards becomes merged, tested code with no person in the middle. v0 covers build and test only.
subtree: 11 cards, 11 open, 4 stale

Six steps.

    1  select     a person picks a subtree and triggers          #werk-loop-ticket
                  ticket planning. Some subtrees are not
                  buildable or are too small — the person judges
    2  plan work  the planner reads the whole subtree, with       #werk-loop-planner
                  access to the whole map, and writes tickets
    3  fan out    one agent per ticket, one worktree each,        #werk-loop-fanout
                  as many at once as independence allows
    4  hand back  each marks its work done and shares a diff.     #werk-loop-land
                  Local, not a real PR, if possible
    5  merge      a coordinator merges the finished, tested       #werk-loop-merge
                  tickets and resolves conflicts
    6  record     what got built goes back on the map             #werk-loop-state

Step 1 is not automated on purpose. A person selects the subtree. Nothing infers buildability from the shape of the refines tree — #werk-loop-unit tried and failed.

`bun test` and `bun run e2e` from #werk-test are the loop's only eyes. Steps 3 and 5 both run them; #werk-loop-done sets the threshold.

**Out of scope.** Graded judgement (#lp-two), rubrics (#lp-rubric), trend limits (#lp-trend), and the outer iterate cycle. Build and test only.

**Existing machinery.** src/prototype.ts runs headless `claude -p` agents in parallel detached worktrees and captures each diff — step 3 and half of step 4. The log takes new event kinds. web/diff.js renders a patch.

**Step 5 has no precedent here.** Every other step has working code or a close cousin in this repo. Nothing has merged N independently-green worktrees.

Test 1 fails. The fork is "frozen ticket set" vs "recomputed each pass". Two sentences state it fully. There is no layout, wording, timing, or rendered thing that a sample would show me that the prose does not.

Test 2 fails too. Three cards push every sample to the same pick, (a) frozen:

1. `#werk-loop-gap` says a mid-build pick "becomes a card: who:prototype, status open", and "after a run, `werk find` shows Eryk what the loop had to invent". That is an after-the-run human read. A run that consumed its own new cards would delete that review point.
2. `#werk-loop-ticket` step 1 makes a person select the subtree and trigger ticket planning. It calls this "the loop's only human gate before the merge — a G2 in #stages terms". Recomputation inside the run walks past that gate.
3. `#werk-loop-gap` files cards with `status open`, not `decided`. `#werk-loop-ticket` derives tickets from decided cards. An open card is not ticket input yet, so the new cards cannot enter the current run by the rules already written.

Two more facts worth passing back, both outside the sampled fork:

- `#werk-loop-done` does not define a run-level exit at all. It defines a **per-ticket** pass: checks pass, checks fail with a retry left, or the cap is reached. On the cap it says "stop the run and leave the branch where it is". So the run already has a documented abort path and no documented success path across N tickets. That gap is larger than the frozen-vs-recomputed question.
- `#werk-loop-ticket` open question 1 ("durable artifact or throwaway the loop regenerates per run?") is the real parent of this fork, and it is a question for Eryk, not for samples. Durable implies frozen. Throwaway-per-run still implies frozen *within* a run unless something says otherwise.

Recommendation: ask Eryk open question 1 on `#werk-loop-ticket` directly, and separately raise that `#werk-loop-done` covers one ticket, not the whole run. Neither needs `prototyper`.

**Three words an agent cannot evaluate as written.**

    ready          Ready means every blocker is built. #werk-loop-ticket

                   runs once after the merge, per #werk-loop-merge, so it is
